Home Shows States Records Project Press Kit

A weekday briefing for every jurisdiction in the nation — the 50 states, the District of Columbia, and the U.S. territories — plus weekly deep dives, district deep dives, section-by-section walkthroughs of the laws that run schools (IDEA, Section 504, and state rules like New Hampshire's Ed 1100), an assessment series, and national investigations built from public records. Hosted by Alex and Jordan.

[NH] NH Education Daily — October 26, 2026: The Costs Nobody Counts

October 26, 2026 · 7:38

▶ Play episode
Episode notes & sources

New Hampshire ranks first in the nation for students on Section 504-only plans at 8.4 percent, more than double the national rate — yet no one at the state or district level tracks what those plans cost, and no state or federal funding follows them. A look at what House Bill 1548's special education cost report would count, the Section 504 question it may leave unanswered, and what district leaders can count themselves this week.

Sources:
- Education Funding's Black Box, 'The Third Rail: Special Education and NH's Property Taxes,' October 23, 2026 (504-only and IEP rates from U.S. Department of Education, Office for Civil Rights, Civil Rights Data Collection 2023-24 public-use file, author's calculations): https://polimom.substack.com/p/the-third-rail-special-education

[American Samoa] Deep Dive — Needs Assistance: The June 2026 IDEA Determinations and the Unfinished Transition Fix

October 25, 2026 · 33:23

▶ Play episode
Episode notes & sources

In June 2026 the U.S. Department of Education told American Samoa, for the second straight year, that its early intervention program needs assistance under IDEA — and the unresolved federal finding underneath that grade is about the handoff at a child's third birthday. Alex and Jordan read the determination letters line by line: how the Results-Driven Accountability score is built, why Specific Conditions on three straight grant awards cap the territory's category, what the September 2024 monitoring finding on Part C-to-Part B transition actually says, how the territory answered with a Transition MOU and nearly finished policy rewrites, why a perfect transition score built on two children does not close a system-design finding, and the two dates that now govern everything — the February 1, 2027 report on technical assistance received and actions taken, and the June 2027 determinations that may formally count longstanding noncompliance. Educational guidance, not legal advice.

[New Hampshire] Deep Dive — State Complaints, ESY, and Compensatory Education

October 23, 2026 · 26:29

▶ Play episode
Episode notes & sources

This deep dive walks through the three dispute tools that meet in one file folder: the state complaint under 34 CFR 300.151 through 300.153 and New Hampshire's Ed 1121 process (who can file, the sixty-day clock, the commissioner's signed decision, the twenty-day reconsideration rule, and the public complaint summaries required by RSA 186-C:5-a); extended school year under 34 CFR 300.106 and New Hampshire's Ed 1110.01 (individual team determination, the regression and recoupment standard, and the factors beyond regression); and compensatory education under the qualitative "but for" standard of Reid v. District of Columbia, 401 F.3d 516 (D.C. Cir. 2005), including the First Circuit's Pihl decision and real New Hampshire complaint orders that required districts to deliver compensatory services. The episode closes with the documentation habits that decide these cases in practice. Plain-English explanations of the governing rules, with settled law distinguished from practical interpretation, for working New Hampshire special education teachers and case managers.

### Sources

- 34 CFR 300.151–300.153 (state complaint procedures, remedies, and filing contents): https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/34/300.152 — also search eCFR at ecfr.gov for "300.151 adoption of State complaint procedures" and "300.153 complaint contents" to read the adopted text of all three sections side by side.
- New Hampshire Rules for the Education of Children with Disabilities, Ed 1121 (complaint process) and Ed 1110.01 (extended school year): full rule text at https://www.gc.nh.gov/rules/state_agencies/ed1100.html — find Ed 1121 in Part Ed 1121 and Ed 1110.01 in Part Ed 1110 on that page; annotated copy with cross-references in the Guide to the NH Standards for the Education of Children with Disabilities at https://picnh.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/Guide-to-the-NH-Standards-3.1.2024.pdf

- RSA 186-C:5-a (state complaint tracking system and required public posting of redacted complaint summaries): https://law.justia.com/codes/new-hampshire/title-xv/chapter-186-c/section-186-c-5-a/
- NH Department of Education, Special Education State Complaint #25-35 (corrective action plan ordering the team to determine missed progress and implement compensatory services): http://doe.nhdoit.acsitefactory.com/sites/g/files/ehbemt326/files/inline-documents/sonh/case-25-35.pdf

Episode notes & sources

Lock the door, pull the shade, move the children to the hard corner. The lockdown drill is rehearsed in every school in America — and it is the closest thing public school teachers have to a workplace safety law. In this national episode, Alex and Jordan trace why: a single definition in the Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970 wrote every public employee in the country out of the nation's workplace-safety law, and the right to a workplace free from recognized hazards stops at the schoolhouse door. We built the count from OSHA's own registry: in 29 of the 56 states, districts, and territories, a public school employee has a real safety regulator; in 27, there is no one to complain to. Plus the bargain police and firefighters got and teachers never did, the IDEA collision that stops abatement where a student is the hazard, New York's 2024 law that proves the fix can be built, and New Hampshire's paper right — a petition process aimed at a rulebook with no violence standard in it. The full written feature and the jurisdiction-by-jurisdiction coverage map are published with this story at educationacrossthestates.com.

Sources — OSHA, State Plans (22 full plans covering private and public sector workers; 7 public-sector-only plans: Connecticut, Illinois, Maine, Massachusetts, New Jersey, New York, U.S. Virgin Islands): https://www.osha.gov/stateplans ; Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970, section 3(5) definition of "employer" and section 5(a)(1) General Duty Clause: https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/oshact/completeoshact and https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/oshact/section5-duties ; Littler, "New York Amends Workplace Violence Prevention Law to Extend Coverage to Public Schools" (Labor Law section 27-b, effective January 4, 2024): https://www.littler.com/news-analysis/asap/new-york-amends-workplace-violence-prevention-law-extend-coverage-public-schools ; Parker & Covert LLP on California SB 553 / Labor Code section 6401.9 (written workplace violence prevention plans, including school districts, by July 1, 2024): https://www.parkercovert.com/new-requirements-for-california-employers-to-implement-workplace-violence-prevention-plans-by-july-2024 ; New Hampshire RSA chapter 277 (277:13-a employee petition for inspection; 277:15-a post-incident inspections naming school districts): https://gc.nh.gov/rsa/html/XXIII/277/277-mrg.htm ; Individuals with Disabilities Education Act discipline provisions, 20 U.S.C. 1415(k): https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/20/1415 ; Bricker & Eckler on Ohio's Public Employment Risk Reduction Program (PERRP, ORC chapter 4167): https://www.brickergraydon.com/insights/publications/PERRP-are-your-employees-safe

On July 1, 2026, New Hampshire's Home Education Freedom Act (HB 1268) took effect - repealing the homeschool notice, the required subjects, the portfolio, and the annual evaluation all at once, and ending the state's count of home educated children. The List Nobody Can See: Inside the Child Care Food Program's Seven-Year Blacklist

October 23, 2026 · 30:30

▶ Play episode
Episode notes & sources

One routine Federal Register notice this fall renewed the paperwork behind the National Disqualified List — the Child and Adult Care Food Program's national bar on institutions, sponsoring organizations, day care home providers, and the individuals who run them. This deep dive opens up the machine: how a review finding becomes a "serious deficiency," how the corrective-action clock runs, why quitting does not save you, the appeal you get — and the six decisions 7 CFR 226.6(k)(3) says you can never appeal — and how a listing lasts seven years, or longer if a program debt is unpaid. Plus the vagueness problem the National CACFP Association put in writing (the same citation can mean a serious management problem in one state or "three small errors on a reimbursement claims form" in another), the patchwork early-removal door, the Feeding Our Future record that explains why the list exists, and the 2024 proposed rule (FNS-2024-0005) that would rebuild the process — still unfinalized. USDA does not publish the list or its size; where the public record runs out, this episode says so.

The Plan Nobody Audits: Section 504's Quiet Quadrupling

October 23, 2026 · 26:08

▶ Play episode
Episode notes & sources

This deep dive examines the fastest-growing accommodation system in American public schools: plans under Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 held by students who do not have IEPs. Drawing on the U.S. Department of Education's Civil Rights Data Collection for 2023–24 and the leading published research, Alex and Jordan walk through what a Section 504 plan is and how its three-part eligibility test differs from the IDEA; how the "504-only" rate climbed from 1.1% of students in 2009–10 to 3.9% in 2021–22 and about 1.9 million students (4%) in 2023–24; why rates range from near double the national average in Texas and New Hampshire to below half in New Mexico and Mississippi, with individual Texas middle schools above 30% and other schools at zero; the documented skew toward White students (60% of 504-only students against 44% of enrollment) and, in the first study to link school records to IRS tax data, toward higher-income families (2.9% vs. 1.5%), even as IEPs run the opposite way; the measured response of 504 enrollment to the College Board's 2017 decision to honor school accommodations on the SAT automatically; the costs of both over-identification and under-identification; and the central evidentiary gap — no national breakdown of 504 plans by condition and no national audit of 504 eligibility has ever been published, so claims about how many plans are "unnecessary" exceed what the evidence can support. Plain-English explanations, with every number sourced and the limits of the evidence stated on air.

### Sources

- U.S. Department of Education, Office for Civil Rights, "A First Look: The Civil Rights Data Collection, 2023–24" (September 2026) — 19% of students with disabilities (15% IDEA; 4% / ~1.9M Section 504 only); White students 60% of 504-only vs. 44% of enrollment; boys 56% of 504-only: https://www.ed.gov/media/document/2023-24-first-look-civil-rights-data-collection-september-30-2026-114593.pdf
- Perry A. Zirkel, "Concerns About Misidentification of '504-Only' Students," ATPE News, March 30, 2026 — 1.1% (2009–10) to 3.9% (2021–22); Texas 7.6%; 23 of the top 25 districts (14.4%–17.4%); Texas middle schools at 23.1%–30.1%; three-part eligibility test; no federal/state funding; costs of over- and under-identification; Texas dyslexia analysis: https://atpenews.org/concerns-about-misidentification-of-504-only-students/
- Perry A. Zirkel, "Mis-identifying '504-Only' Students," eSchool News, February 6, 2026 — New Hampshire and Texas at almost double the national rate; New Mexico and Mississippi at less than half; California 2.1% with districts ranging 0%–13.9% and schools 0%–24.2%: https://www.eschoolnews.com/innovative-teaching/2026/02/06/mis-identifying-504-only-students/
- Zirkel et al., analysis of the 2009–10 Civil Rights Data Collection, Journal of Disability Policy Studies (2014), reported by Education Week — 504-only rates: White 1.26%, Black 0.57%, Hispanic 0.50%; Title I schools 0.84% vs. non-Title I 1.23%: https://www.edweek.org/teaching-learning/students-with-504-plans-more-likely-to-be-white-enrolled-in-non-title-i-schools/2014/08
- Holler & Zirkel, national survey of Section 504-only students (2008), reported by Education Week — mid-2000s rate of about 1.2%; ADHD the most commonly listed impairment, diabetes next: https://www.edweek.org/teaching-learning/counting-section-504-students/2008/03
- Ainsworth et al., Oregon study linking school records (2008–09 to 2018–19) to IRS tax data (paper released January 2026), and Tiffany Liu, study of 504 enrollment after the College Board's 2017 SAT accommodation policy (March 2026), both reported by The 74 / Disability Scoop, June 9, 2026 — 504 receipt 2.9% near the top of the income distribution vs. 1.5% near the bottom; IEP receipt about 25% among the most disadvantaged; verbatim comments from Nick Ainsworth, Paul Morgan, Ben Lovett, Miriam Nunberg, and Christopher Cleveland: https://www.disabilityscoop.com/2026/06/09/wealthy-students-more-likely-to-get-disability-accommodations-study-finds/32038/
- Tiffany Liu's College Board finding as also reported by Education Daly — the 504 enrollment response about 24% larger in the most affluent communities than in high-poverty schools: https://www.educationdaly.us/p/we-need-to-talk-about-504-plans
